section_summary: This section documents the severe political crisis in Japan precipitated by the assassination of Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai during the May 15 Incident of 1932 and its international repercussions. It contains extensive diplomatic despatches, cross-reference sheets, and telegrams detailing Japanese ultra-nationalist societies, bitter disputes between the Seiyukai Cabinet and the military over the South Manchuria Railway, and growing domestic agitation favoring withdrawal from the League of Nations. Despatches from Tokyo, Peiping, Shanghai, and Washington chronicle the collapse of party government, Chinese and Soviet anxieties over Japanese military expansion, and the eventual installation of a transitional national coalition ministry under Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito.

subfiles.about: Roster and analytical profiles of Japanese nationalist, reactionary, patriotic, and state-socialist organizations transmitted as enclosures to Despatch No. 588.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document comprises two detailed enclosures to Tokyo Despatch No. 588 surveying reactionary and nationalist societies in Japan. The first part concludes an extensive numerical catalogue (entries 55 through 124) listing organization names, English translations, founding dates, headquarters, leaders, publications, and memberships. The second enclosure provides comprehensive profiles of seven leading reactionary bodies: Dai Nippon Kokusui-kai, Dai Nippon Seigi-dan, Dai Nippon Seisan-to, Kenkoku-kai, Kokuryu-kai (Black Dragon Society), Nippon Shakai-Shugi Kenkyu-jo, and Zen-Nippon Aikokusha Kyodotoso Kyogikai. The report emphasizes the groups' monarchist tenets, anti-communist agitation, rejection of parliamentary capitalism, advocacy of state socialism, and growing sympathy among junior army and naval officers.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 588: Reactionary and Nationalist Organizations in Japan (Enclosures)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 586 concerning the dismissal of South Manchuria Railway Vice President Eguchi.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 586, filed under decimal file 893.22/2857 and recorded in 894.00/386. It notes that the despatch reports on the dismissal of Vice President Eguchi of the South Manchuria Railway by the Japanese Government. It further indicates that the despatch analyzes the resulting public and political reaction.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding South Manchuria Railway Vice President Eguchi Dismissal (Despatch No. 586)

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the dismissal of South Manchuria Railway Vice President Teijo Eguchi, Count Uchida's resignation, and the resulting clash between the Seiyukai Cabinet and the military.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 586 reports that the Seiyukai Cabinet obtained an Imperial ordinance dismissing Teijo Eguchi as Vice President of the South Manchuria Railway, prompting Railway President Count Yasuya Uchida and several directors to submit their resignations. The action drew fierce public and editorial condemnation against the Inukai administration for subordinating national interests in Manchuria to partisan spoils. Japanese military authorities in Kwantung and War Minister Sadao Araki strongly objected to party interference and blocked the appointment of Seiyukai politician Jotaro Yamamoto, insisting that railway management cooperate strictly with military policy. The despatch includes a translated editorial from the Hochi Shimbun entitled 'Tyranny of Seiyukai,' which excoriates the government's despotic methods and partisan corruption.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 586: Dismissal of Vice President Eguchi of the South Manchuria Railway

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 590 concerning Cabinet approval of a supplementary budget for peace preservation expenditures.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 590, filed under decimal file 894.51/357 and indexed under 894.00/387. The note records that the Japanese Cabinet approved the submission of a supplementary budget to the Diet. The budget included appropriations for peace preservation and security measures necessitated by recent political and financial assassinations.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Supplementary Budget for Peace Preservation (Despatch No. 590)

subfiles.about: Urgent telegram reporting the shooting of Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai, attacks on Count Makino's residence, and bombings across Tokyo during the May 15 Incident.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 126 reports that the Japanese Foreign Office orally informed the American Embassy that Prime Minister Inukai was shot and critically wounded early on the evening of May 15, 1932. Attackers dressed in military and naval uniforms drove through Tokyo in several automobiles, attacking the residence of Count Makino (who escaped unharmed), firing on the Metropolitan Police headquarters, and bombing Seiyukai party headquarters. About eighteen perpetrators surrendered or were apprehended, identifying themselves as members of a young officers' association dedicated to combating corruption, weakness in governance, and capitalism. Neville reports that Tokyo remains otherwise quiet, with no evidence of anti-foreign hostility or danger to American citizens.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 126 from Tokyo reporting the Assassination of Prime Minister Inukai (May 15 Incident)

subfiles.about: Telegraphic instruction to the American Embassy in Tokyo to express condolences on the shooting of Prime Minister Inukai.
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr. (Acting Secretary of State), Department of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: This telegram from the Department of State directs the American Embassy in Tokyo to extend official condolences on behalf of the United States Government following the attack on Prime Minister Inukai. It instructs the Chargé d'Affaires to convey profound sympathy to the Japanese authorities. The instructions were subsequently carried out as reported in Tokyo's telegram No. 128.
subfiles.title: Telegram from State Department to Tokyo Expressing Condolences on Prime Minister Inukai's Death

subfiles.about: Telegram confirming execution of condolence instructions and reporting the collective resignation of the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 128 reports that the Department's instructions regarding official condolences on the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai were duly carried out. Neville states that while the capital remains outwardly calm, the Japanese Cabinet has just submitted its formal resignation. He notes that it is still too early to provide a definitive assessment of future political developments.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 128 from Tokyo regarding Cabinet Resignation following Inukai Assassination

subfiles.about: Telegram from former Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes requesting the State Department to cable personal condolences to Foreign Minister Yoshizawa.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, Boston, Massachusetts
subfiles.summary: W. Cameron Forbes, former American Ambassador to Japan then staying in Boston, requests the State Department to transmit a cable to Chargé d'Affaires Neville at Forbes's personal expense. The message asks Neville to convey to Foreign Minister Kenkichi Yoshizawa Forbes's profound personal regret over the terrible tragedy of Prime Minister Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.title: Telegram from W. Cameron Forbes to State Department Requesting Message of Regret to Yoshizawa

subfiles.about: Instruction relaying former Ambassador Forbes's personal message of sympathy to Japanese Foreign Minister Kenkichi Yoshizawa.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson transmits the text of former Ambassador Forbes's condolence message to the American Embassy in Tokyo. Neville is instructed to deliver the message directly to Foreign Minister Yoshizawa, expressing Forbes's deep regret regarding the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai.
subfiles.title: Telegram from State Department to Tokyo Relaying Forbes's Message to Yoshizawa

subfiles.about: Report on post-assassination political negotiations, Genro Saionji's summons to Tokyo, and military opposition to party government.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 132 reports that no new government has yet been formed following Inukai's assassination and the Cabinet's resignation. The Emperor has summoned Genro Prince Saionji to Tokyo to advise on the selection of a new Premier. Neville notes intense opposition to party government, with army officers insisting they will not cooperate with any party administration, while Finance Minister Korekiyo Takahashi serves as provisional Prime Minister amid general political hesitation to accept office.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 132 from Tokyo on Political Crisis and Formation of New Government

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 560 explaining Home Minister Nakahashi's resignation over the Sakuradamon Incident.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 560, filed under 894.00 P.R./52 and recorded under 894.00/392. It notes that the resignation of Mr. Nakahashi as Minister for Home Affairs was actually a delayed consequence of the Sakurada Mon Affair of January 1932. Under Japanese political doctrine, Nakahashi was forced to bear official responsibility for the assassination attempt against the Emperor.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Resignation of Home Minister Nakahashi (Despatch No. 560)

subfiles.about: Telegram quoting a Moscow broadcast by the Red Army Chief of Staff analyzing Inukai's murder and Soviet-Japanese relations.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 541 quotes a Transocean-Asiatic dispatch from Moscow summarizing a radio address by the Chief of the General Staff of the Red Army concerning Prime Minister Inukai's assassination. The Soviet general linked the killings of French President Doumer and Inukai to anti-Soviet hostility, observing that Inukai had opposed an anti-Soviet policy and restrained aggressive Japanese officers in Manchuria. The speaker declared that while Soviet diplomacy would seek peaceful relations, an understanding with the Japanese military caste was impossible, warning that the coming weeks would show whether diplomats or soldiers dictate Japanese policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 541 from Peiping Quoting Soviet Reaction to Inukai's Assassination

subfiles.about: Extensive compilation of Chinese vernacular and foreign press commentary on the assassination of Premier Inukai and the rise of Japanese fascism.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 548 transmits comprehensive extracts of Chinese and foreign editorial opinion across Shanghai, Peiping, Tientsin, Canton, and Nanking regarding Inukai's assassination. Major newspapers including China Times, Shun Pao, Sin Wan Pao, North China Daily News, China Press, Ta Kung Pao, and Central Daily News interpreted the outrage as a fascist military coup aimed at overthrowing parliamentary government, annexing Manchuria and Mongolia, and pursuing war with Soviet Russia and the United States. Commentators underscored the irony of Japan portraying China as an unorganized state when Tokyo could not protect its own Premier in his official residence. The press concluded that Inukai's removal foreshadows an aggressive military dictatorship and heightened military pressure on China.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 548 from Peiping Relaying Chinese and Foreign Press Reactions to Inukai's Assassination

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Telegram No. 549 regarding Wang Ching-wei's concerns over the establishment of a military government in Japan.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references Peiping Telegram No. 549, filed under 793.94/5241 and indexed under 894.00/395. It notes that Wang Ching-wei expressed grave concern that the establishment of a military regime in Japan following Inukai's assassination would further aggravate Sino-Japanese relations.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Wang Ching-wei's Fears of Japanese Military Government (Telegram No. 549)

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting Kuo Wen report of an interview with Executive Yuan President Wang Ching-wei on talks with Akira Ariyoshi and domestic political reform.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 549 transmits a Kuo Wen news report of an interview with Wang Ching-wei, Chairman of the Executive Yuan, in Nanking. Wang stated that his discussion with visiting Japanese diplomat Akira Ariyoshi touched on the Chinese boycott movement, which Wang maintained was the direct consequence of Japanese aggression in Manchuria and could only cease if Japan reversed its policy. Wang described Inukai's assassination as deeply unfortunate, warning that a military government in Japan would severely worsen the situation, while also reviewing domestic Kuomintang affairs and Sun Fo's reform proposals.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 549 from Peiping reporting Wang Ching-wei's Press Interview on Inukai's Death and Ariyoshi's Visit

subfiles.about: Report quoting Nippon Dempo on younger Japanese army officers' uncompromising rejection of party government and their thirteen demands.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 553 relays a Nippon Dempo press report from Tokyo describing the unyielding determination of younger military officers to reject any future party-based administration. War Minister Sadao Araki and Vice Chief of Staff Masaki are reported powerless to moderate the young officers, rendering Kisaburo Suzuki's prospects of forming a Seiyukai Cabinet highly doubtful. A faction of junior officers presented a formal memorial to General Araki demanding that no existing political party participate in the new cabinet and putting forward thirteen specific policy demands.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 553 from Peiping reporting Military Demands and Opposition to Party Government

subfiles.about: Confidential report on rumors linking officer suicides and battlefield deaths in China to the October 1931 coup and Blood Brotherhood assassinations.
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Dickover reports a confidential rumor concerning recent press accounts of Japanese army officers committing suicide in China under the guise of ultra-patriotism. The account alleges that military authorities avoided publicly court-martialing officers implicated in the abortive October 1931 coup by sending them to China to be killed or commit suicide. Furthermore, it is alleged that an aviation officer killed in China had supplied the firearms used by the Blood Brotherhood to assassinate Junnosuke Inouye and Baron Takuma Dan, suggesting he was deliberately eliminated to prevent exposure of wider military complicity.
subfiles.title: Letter from Consul Dickover to Neville regarding Rumors on Officer Suicides and Blood Brotherhood Assassinations
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Official record of discussion between Secretary Stimson and Ambassador Debuchi regarding condolences, cabinet reorganization, and Shanghai troop withdrawals.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: This memorandum records a meeting between Secretary of State Stimson and Japanese Ambassador Katsuji Debuchi, who called to express Japan's gratitude for American condolence messages following Inukai's assassination. Debuchi assured Stimson that while the reorganization of the Japanese Government was not yet settled, it would not be a fascist regime, though it might take the form of a national coalition. Debuchi further affirmed that Japan was determined to carry out its troop withdrawal from Shanghai regardless of cabinet changes, and touched briefly on a proposed international round table conference.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Secretary of State Stimson and Japanese Ambassador Debuchi

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential instruction transmitting to Chargé Neville a copy of Secretary Stimson's conversation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 322 encloses for the personal and confidential information of Chargé d'Affaires Neville a copy of Secretary Stimson's May 19 memorandum of conversation with Ambassador Debuchi. The transmission covers the political reorganization of the Japanese Government and the proposed round table conference. Neville is specifically instructed not to distribute the document to his embassy staff.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 322 from Secretary Stimson to Neville Transmitting Debuchi Memorandum
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential instruction transmitting to Minister Johnson a copy of Secretary Stimson's conversation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Secretary Stimson forwards a confidential copy of his May 19 conversation with Japanese Ambassador Debuchi to Minister Nelson T. Johnson in Peiping. The document reviews the Japanese cabinet crisis and the proposed round table conference. Johnson is authorized, at his discretion, to make the memorandum available to the Counselors of the Legation.
subfiles.title: Instruction from Secretary Stimson to Johnson Transmitting Debuchi Memorandum
subfiles.to: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito received the Imperial command to form a compromise national cabinet.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 136 announces that Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito received the Imperial command to form a new Cabinet on the evening of May 22, 1932. Saito's selection is regarded as a compromise between extreme nationalism and political partisanship, rendering him acceptable to the military, political parties, and the public. Although the press expresses regret at the departure from party government, the appointment is widely welcomed as necessary under existing national difficulties.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 136 from Tokyo reporting Imperial Command to Admiral Saito to Form Cabinet

subfiles.about: Inquiry from Minister Johnson whether the State Department desires summaries of Tokyo press reports received in Peiping repeated via naval radio.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 561 notes that news agencies including Reuter's, Rengo, and Nippon Dempo are carrying extensive coverage of Tokyo political developments in Peiping. Minister Johnson inquires whether the Department of State wishes the Legation to repeat texts or summaries of these press reports utilizing naval radio facilities at no expense.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 561 from Peiping Inquiring on Transmission of Tokyo Press Reports via Naval Radio

subfiles.about: State Department instruction requesting the Peiping Legation to transmit texts and summaries of Tokyo press reports via naval radio.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: In reply to Legation Telegram No. 561, the Department of State instructs Minister Johnson to transmit by naval radio the texts or summaries of important press reports from Tokyo regarding the Japanese political crisis.
subfiles.title: Telegram from State Department to Peiping Requesting Tokyo Press Reports by Naval Radio

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that rumors of the death of General Yoshinori Shirakawa in Shanghai are premature.
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Cunningham, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 262 reports that the Japanese Consul General informed Consul General Cunningham that rumors regarding the death of General Yoshinori Shirakawa (wounded in the Hongkew Park bombing) are, to say the least, premature. The information was also repeated to the American Legation in Peiping.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 262 from Shanghai regarding False Rumor of General Shirakawa's Death

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 611 concerning press agitation in Japan favoring withdrawal from the League of Nations.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 611, filed under 793.94/5251 and indexed under 894.00/402. The note highlights that the despatch examines strong public and press sentiment in Japan favoring withdrawal from the League of Nations in the wake of the Manchurian dispute.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Press Comment on Japan's Possible Withdrawal from the League of Nations (Despatch No. 611)

subfiles.about: Analysis of mounting Japanese agitation to withdraw from the League of Nations, featuring translations of press articles and a cautionary critique by Dr. Hitoshi Ashida.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 611 examines intense public and military agitation in Japan advocating secession from the League of Nations. Neville highlights militant speeches by War Minister Sadao Araki and editorial series in the Osaka Mainichi arguing that the League is an obstructive European body that fails to understand Far Eastern realities. The despatch includes two translated enclosures: an article outlining the economic perils and treaty complications of withdrawal, and a penetrating essay by former diplomat Dr. Hitoshi Ashida entitled 'Japan's Diplomacy at a Turning Point.' Ashida urges prudence, comparing Japan's current war fever to pre-war imperial Germany and warning that quitting the League would surrender Japan's permanent Council seat, forfeit mandatory authority over the South Sea Islands, and invite catastrophic international isolation.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 611: Press Comment regarding Possibility of Withdrawal by Japan from the League of Nations

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Telegram No. 556 concerning Akira Ariyoshi's conversations with Wang Ching-wei and Lo Wen-kan.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references Peiping Telegram No. 556, filed under 793.94/5346 and recorded under 894.00/403. It notes that Akira Ariyoshi called on Wang Ching-wei and Lo Wen-kan in Nanking, confined his remarks to generalities, and departed promptly upon learning of Prime Minister Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Ariyoshi's Conversations with Wang Ching-wei and Lo Wen-kan (Telegram No. 556)

subfiles.about: Report transmitting Nanking findings that Akira Ariyoshi had acted as a direct personal emissary of the late Premier Inukai.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 556 relays a message from the American Consul General at Nanking stating that Akira Ariyoshi had traveled as a confidential emissary of Prime Minister Inukai, similar to Yosuke Matsuoka. Because Inukai was assassinated on the day of Ariyoshi's arrival in Nanking, Ariyoshi confined his conversations with Wang Ching-wei and Foreign Minister Lo Wen-kan to broad generalities and departed immediately for Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 556 from Peiping transmitting Nanking Report on Ariyoshi's Mission as Inukai's Emissary

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 600 containing the Japan monthly political report for April 1932.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 600, filed under 894.00 P.R./53 and recorded under 894.00/404. It summarizes the report's conclusion that the general political situation in Japan showed no prospect of improvement and that the ruling Seiyukai party faced intense adverse criticism throughout April 1932.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding General Political Situation and Criticisms of Seiyukai (Despatch No. 600)

subfiles.about: Embassy report extract detailing the deepening crisis of the Inukai Cabinet, economic distress, Minseito platform changes, and growing attraction to fascism.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 600 (Political Report for April 1932) details the acute difficulties confronting Prime Minister Inukai's administration. Worsening economic conditions and the arbitrary dismissal of SMR Vice President Eguchi—prompting Count Uchida's resignation—provoked intense public and press condemnation for political opportunism during a national emergency. Meanwhile, Baron Wakatsuki led the opposition Minseito to drop the return to the gold standard from its platform, and widespread social unrest stimulated strong public interest in fascism, extreme reactionary organizations, and a brewing split within the Social Democratic Party.
subfiles.title: Extract from Despatch No. 600: Political Report for April 1932 (General Political Situation and Opposition Activities)

subfiles.about: Report on the formal installation of Viscount Saito's national coalition cabinet and plans to convene an extraordinary Diet session.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 141 announces that the new cabinet headed by Viscount Makoto Saito was formally installed on the afternoon of May 26, 1932. Viscount Saito will temporarily hold the portfolio of Foreign Affairs concurrently with the premiership. Neville notes that the Diet is expected to convene the following week to address emergency relief plans, and observes that the new ministry comprises members of both major parties alongside non-partisan figures.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 141 from Tokyo reporting Installation of the Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: Transmission of Japanese press reports detailing the ministerial roster of the Saito Cabinet and initial reactions from political, financial, and military circles.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 571 relays Nippon Dempo news dispatches from Tokyo providing the complete ministerial line-up of Viscount Saito's newly formed cabinet: Tatsuo Yamamoto (Home), Korekiyo Takahashi (Finance), Senjuro Hayashi (War), Keisuke Okada (Navy), Matsukichi Koyama (Justice), Ichiro Hatoyama (Education), Fumio Goto (Agriculture), Kumakichi Nakajima (Commerce and Industry), Hiroshi Minami (Communications), Chuzo Mitsuchi (Railways), Ryutaro Nagai (Overseas), Zenzaburo Shibata (Chief Cabinet Secretary), and Zenjiro Horikiri (Legislative Bureau). Commentary indicates that the public and business communities are disappointed by the selection of second-tier figures, while predicting friction between Minseito and Seiyukai ministers and noting that the military accepts the arrangement merely as a transitional non-party ministry.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 571 from Peiping transmitting Nippon Dempo Reports on Saito Cabinet Line-up and Public Reception

subfiles.about: Transmission of a Reuter dispatch from Tokyo detailing administrative reshuffles, military promotions, and party alignments under the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 572 transmits a Reuter dispatch from Tokyo detailing administrative appointments accompanying the formation of the Saito Ministry, including Count Hideo Kodama as Governor-General of Formosa, General Yoshiyuki Kawashima as Commander-in-Chief in Korea, and Prince Fushimi's promotion to Fleet Admiral on the anniversary of the Battle of Tsushima. The report evaluates the balance of power within the cabinet, which includes three Seiyukai ministers, two Minseito ministers, and several non-party figures with known political leanings. It notes widespread public relief at the conclusion of the cabinet crisis, while suggesting that Count Yasuya Uchida may still be persuaded to accept the Foreign Affairs portfolio upon his upcoming visit to Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 572 from Peiping transmitting Reuter Report on Military and Administrative Appointments under Saito Cabinet
